newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa rand at new low and no end in sight.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa rand at new low and no end in sight.

text.p: South Africa's battered currency tumbled to new lows on Monday and some analysts said it could soon cost five rands to buy one dollar.

The rand sank to an all-time low of 4.67 bid against the U.S. unit in late trade and broke through 7.50 against the British pound, taking its toll on shares and the bond market, where yields hit a five-month high.

Foreign exchange dealers said the speculative attack on the rand appeared relentless as the currency shed a further five cents of its value against the dollar on Monday, bringing its loss to more than 100 cents since February 15 this year.

There were fears that the sell-off might force the central Reserve Bank to raise interest rates to defend the currency but Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said he was not contemplating an imminent hike.
Stals told Reuters he planned to hold his hand on rates after September money supply data showed some stabilisation.
"It confirms that we maintain the status quo for the time being," Stals said.
"We are looking for indications that it will come down to a lower rate of increase but at least it is encouraging that the rate is not increasing further."
Broadly defined M3 money supply grew 14.45 percent in September, down from 15.40 in August, while private credit extension expanded 17.94 percent from 17.70.
Stals had warned in a speech on Friday that already high interest rates might have to be raised further if there was no slowdown in money supply and credit growth.

Dealers said most of the pressure on the rand came from overseas investors, fearful that the country's economic problems -- including balance of payments difficulties and low reserves -- would not be solved any time soon.
London-based analysts said the rand would continue to take a beating on foreign exchanges in coming months with the economic backdrop failing to improve quickly enough to come to its aid.
Chris Tinker, chief economist treasury at Standard Chartered in London, said the rand could get down to 5.00 over the next six months.
"After that we could trade to 5.25 but if we get there we would probably get back to 5.00 quite quickly. Around 5.00 is that sort of level where anything weaker really isn't sustainable," he said.

The rand has now lost 28 percent of its value against the dollar since mid-February when the run on the currency first started on ill-founded rumours about President Nelson Mandela's heatth and talk of an imminent scrapping of exchange controls.
Since then the Reserve Bank's foreign reserves have fallen by some 50 percent in dollar terms to 10.0 billion rand ($2.2 billion) at the end of September.
That leaves the central bank with little ammunition in its armoury to fight speculative attacks.

Stals said he expected the country's balance of payments position to stablise and start improving, helped by a slowdown in gross domestic expenditure, the depreciation in the rand and the increasing effect of tight domestic financial conditions.
But he said the current account deficit was likely to remain around 12 billion rand in calendar 1996, little changed from 1995's shortfall of 12.7 billion rand.
Bank rate, which currently stands at 16 percent, was last hiked by one percentage point on April 26 this year. Commercial banks' prime lending rate currently stands at 19.25 percent.
